item.title: Elder Sabbhakāma: This two-footed creature, Impure and foul-smelling, Full of various corpses — From it, fluid oozes. With deer, use a trap; with fish, a…
item.description:
Elder Sabbhakāma:

This two-footed creature,
Impure and foul-smelling,
Full of various corpses —
From it, fluid oozes.

With deer, use a trap; with fish, a hook;
With monkeys, a pit;
Thus worldlings are caught.

Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, touches —
Agreeable and pleasing —
These five strands of sensual pleasure
Are known in female form.

Worldlings, with mind infatuated,
Run after enjoying female form.
The terrifying cemetery increases,
Storing up renewed existence.

One who avoids female form
As a foot avoids a snake’s head —
That mindful one overcomes
The world’s poisoner.

Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures,
Security in renunciation,
Having escaped all sensual pleasures,
I have attained the destruction of defilements.

From: Theragāthā 6.14

item.title: “Monks, these six sense bases — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness. What six? The eye sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained…
item.description:
“Monks, these six sense bases — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness. What six? The eye sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — brings happiness. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — brings happiness. These six sense bases, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.94

item.title: … Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: Life is swept along, Short is the lifespan…
item.description:
… Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Do meritorious deeds
That bring true happiness.

(The Blessed One):
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Seeking peace, abandon worldly hopes.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.3

item.title: “Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s…
item.description:
“Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s followers. ‘Herd of deer’ is a synonym for ascetics and brahmins. Here, monks, the first kind of ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, eat the bait cast by Māra and the world’s offerings. Having entered and indulged, they eat those foods, become infatuated; from infatuation, they become heedless; from heedlessness, they become subject to Māra’s will among that bait and those offerings. Thus, monks, these first ascetics and brahmins have not escaped Māra’s power.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta

item.title: “Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and…
item.description:
“Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and humans delight in sound … in odor … in taste … in touch … in phenomena, are excited by phenomena. When phenomena change, fade, and cease, devas and humans dwell in suffering.

Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches,
And all phenomena —
Desirable, delightful, agreeable —
Thus they are called.

Devas and humans in the world,
Regarding them as delightful —
Where they cease and fade away,
Devas and humans see suffering.

The noble one sees as ease
When identity view is destroyed —
The noble one sees as opposite
All the views of the world.

What others call pleasure,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as pleasure.

See the Dhamma, hard to comprehend,
Where the ignorant are bewildered —
Darkness for the blind,
Obscurity for those who cannot see.

The wise are open-eyed,
Like light clearly shining,
The foolish, even though near,
Do not understand the Dhamma.

Overcome by the thirst of birth,
Swept away by the current of existence,
Subject to Māra’s control —
They do not awaken to this Dhamma.

Apart from the noble ones, no one
Awakens to this path —
The path leading to Nibbāna,
With perfect wisdom, free from defilements.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.136

item.title: - What binds the world? What leads the world? By abandoning what thing Is Nibbāna called? - Delight binds the world, Seeking leads the world,…
item.description:
- What binds the world?
What leads the world?
By abandoning what thing
Is Nibbāna called?
- Delight binds the world,
Seeking leads the world,
By abandoning craving,
Is Nibbāna called.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.64

item.title: “Monks, form is burning; feeling is burning; perception is burning; formations are burning; consciousness is burning. Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted…
item.description:
“Monks, form is burning; feeling is burning; perception is burning; formations are burning; consciousness is burning. Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … with feeling … with perception … with formations … with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.61

item.title: “‘The world is deficient, longing, a slave to craving’ — that, great king, is the fourth exposition of the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One,…
item.description:
“‘The world is deficient, longing, a slave to craving’ — that, great king, is the fourth exposition of the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having known, seen, and heard that exposition, I went forth from the household life into homelessness.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by…
item.description:
“Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by nature has strong lust, and he constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of lust. By nature he has strong ill-will, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of ill-will. By nature he has strong delusion, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of delusion. With pain and grief, with tearful face and crying, he lives the holy life that is fully complete and pure. At the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in this realm. This, monks, is called a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 45 – Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta

item.title: - “Venerable sir, I do not understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One regarding the purpose of purity of virtue.” - “Monk, if you…
item.description:
- “Venerable sir, I do not understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One regarding the purpose of purity of virtue.” - “Monk, if you do not understand the Dhamma I have taught regarding the purpose of purity of virtue, then how, monk, do you understand the Dhamma I have taught?” - “Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One as greed and the removal of greed.” - “Good, good, monk! Good, monk! You understand the Dhamma taught by me as greed and the removal of greed. It is for the purpose of greed and the removal of greed, monk, that the Dhamma is taught by me. What do you think, monk: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?” - “Impermanent, venerable sir.” - “The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … Is the mind permanent or impermanent?” - “Impermanent, venerable sir.” - “What is impermanent — is that suffering or happiness?” - “Suffering, venerable sir.” - “What is impermanent, suffering, subject to change — is it fitting to regard it as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” - “No, venerable sir.” - “Seeing thus, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … disenchanted with the mind … Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.74
